1.assumed: The ampere is an SI base unit; volt, ohm and coulomb are derived.

2.assumed: Constructive interference needs a path difference of a whole number of wavelengths.

3.assumed: R ∝ L at fixed area; number density depends only on the material.

4.assumed: Polarised light through a filter at 90° is blocked; at 180° it passes fully again.

5.assumed: Add series resistances; combine parallel branches by reciprocals.

6.assumed: Points in adjacent loops of a stationary wave oscillate in antiphase (π).

7.assumed: Higher intensity means more photons per second, so more electrons per second, same KEmax.

8.assumed: Significant diffraction needs wavelength comparable to gap; microwaves are centimetre-scale.

9.assumed: Third-law pairs are equal, opposite, same type, and act on different bodies.

10.assumed: In any collision with no external force total momentum is conserved; kinetic energy only if elastic.

11.assumed: Currents into a junction must sum to currents out.

12.assumed: Double slits show diffraction, interference and wave nature; refraction is not involved.

13.assumed: x is one fringe spacing: total width ÷ number of spacings; λ = ax/D with mm converted.

14.assumed: Node spacing is λ/2; f = v/λ.

15.assumed: E = ½kx²; compressing a spring increases its stored energy.

16.assumed: Brittle materials show a straight-line stress–strain graph ending abruptly with no plastic region.

17.assumed: E.m.f. is energy transferred to electrical form per unit charge passing through the source.

18.assumed: Find critical angle from sin C = 1/n, compare with incidence angle to normal.

19.assumed: For a product, percentage uncertainties add.

20.assumed: Upthrust = weight of water displaced = mass displaced × g.

21(a).assumed: Series cells add e.m.f. and internal resistance; terminal p.d. V = 3ε − 3Ir; P = IV.

21(b).assumed: Larger r wastes more power (I²r) inside the battery, leaving less for the bulb.

22(a).assumed: Only the component along the motion does work: W = Fx cos θ; P = W/t.

22(b).assumed: Moment = weight × perpendicular distance, unit N m.

22(c).assumed: Smaller perpendicular distance means smaller moment, so spine muscles need less force to balance it.

23(a).assumed: Ammeter in series, voltmeter across thermistor; record temperature, V and I at intervals; R = V/I.

23(b).assumed: Read thermistor resistance and LED switch-on p.d. from graphs; divider output must exceed switch-on p.d.

24(a).assumed: Drag increases with speed until it balances weight; zero resultant gives zero acceleration.

24(b).assumed: v² = u² + 2as from rest with a = g (or mgh = ½mv²).

24(c).assumed: Average repeated times, then use s = ½gt² rearranged for g.

24(d).assumed: Electronic timing removes reaction time; larger drop height reduces percentage uncertainty in time.

24(e).assumed: Height–time graph has gradient equal to velocity: steepens falling, flattens rising; rebound lower due to energy loss.

25(a).assumed: KEmax is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons.

25(b).assumed: Photons each free one electron from the plate; losing negative charge makes the leaf fall.

25(c).assumed: Below threshold one photon's energy is less than the work function, so no electron escapes.

26(a).assumed: Shielding ambient light makes it easier to see when the LED just starts to glow.

26(b).assumed: eV = hf, so gradient of V against f is h/e; multiply gradient by e.

26(c).assumed: Percentage difference = size of (accepted − measured) ÷ accepted × 100.

26(d).assumed: Photon energy hf; photons per second = power ÷ photon energy; compare.
